📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robby Stein, vice president of product for Google Search, announced on November 19, 2026, that Google is globally rolling out a collapsible sidebar on its desktop homepage for finding and resuming recent AI searches.

The change is aimed at searches that develop over multiple exchanges rather than ending after one response. Stein said Search is receiving more of these queries and that, in testing, the sidebar helped people make progress and continue exploring the web. The rollout puts returning to an existing line of inquiry on the same starting surface as beginning a latest search.

AI Mode supplies the experience behind those searches. It produces AI-powered responses with links to web sources and supports follow-up questions. To assemble a response, it runs simultaneous searches across subtopics within a question, a process Google calls query fan-out. The AI Mode documentation describes tasks such as exploring a concept or comparing options that might otherwise require several separate searches.

Questions can be submitted with text, voice, images, PDFs, local or Drive files, and webpage URLs, so a resumable search can involve more than a typed query. Earlier work can also be reopened through AI Mode history. The documentation cautions that AI Mode can misinterpret web content or miss context and recommends checking notable information in more than one place.

Continuity depends on account settings. For the best experience, Google tells owners to enable history and personalized recommendations; without those settings, AI Mode remains available but cannot resume previous searches. On Workspace accounts where Search and Assistant is turned off, Search history is unavailable unless an administrator enables it through the Admin console. Settings for supervised children’s accounts can be managed through Family Link.

Sources indicate that desktop customers can delete individual searches or their entire AI Mode history from the history panel, or remove AI Mode activity through Search History. Deleted items may remain visible in My Activity temporarily, but Google says they are automatically deleted in less than 24 hours and can also be removed manually. An interaction that starts with an AI Overview and continues in AI Mode can create a second history entry, so removing the AI Mode item does not remove the original Search history record.

According to recent reports, the history panel also houses notebooks in AI Mode, which organize projects and research. People can attach files, website URLs or copied text as sources, add custom instructions, search recent threads and place an AI Mode thread in a notebook. Sources and instructions synchronize across AI Mode, Gemini and Gemini Notebook, but conversations from the latter two services do not synchronize into AI Mode.

Recent findings suggest that deleting a notebook in AI Mode also removes it from Gemini and Gemini Notebook along with its sources, while its AI Mode threads return to the Recent threads list. Google states that notebook sources are not used directly to train its generative AI models; separately, AI Mode threads in notebooks may be saved to Search history and used for purposes including showing ads and improving those models, depending on settings.

In a recent development, the rollout makes saved context part of the homepage’s function. Users gain a shorter route back into multi-step research, while the settings governing history, synchronization and deletion determine how much of that context remains available across Google’s AI products.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Early findings point to core-stage underperformance, while solid boosters and Centaur appear to have worked as intended.
  • United Launch Alliance (ULA) says poor booster performance appears to have doomed Sunday's Vulcan mission, which lost an Amazon Leo satellite payload on the rocket's return to flight.
  • ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early findings point to core-stage underperformance, while solid boosters and Centaur appear to have worked as intended.

United Launch Alliance (ULA) says poor booster performance appears to have doomed Sunday's Vulcan mission, which lost an Amazon Leo satellite payload on the rocket's return to flight.

ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately. "Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance," it stated. As a result, stage separation occurred at too low an altitude, and the rocket was not traveling fast enough for the payload to reach orbit.

The second stage appeared to perform well, with its RL10 engines operating as planned, but that wasn't enough to make up for the shortfall, and the mission failed. ULA lost telemetry approximately ten minutes into flight.

Industry observers note that an investigation is underway, led by ULA and overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which had to activate two Debris Response Areas where debris was falling. The agency directs aircraft to leave these areas, and others are prevented from entering.

Industry observers note that late Wednesday afternoon GMT, ULA posted an update stating that it looks like it might be the fuel supply rather than the BE-4 engines that caused the underperformance of the booster. The company wrote: “Preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.".

According to recent reports, previous flights had been blighted by problems with the solid rocket boosters, designed to give the rocket a kick at launch. Those problems prompted a stand-down while investigators examined the cause. This time, ULA said: "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch.".

According to recent reports, attention therefore turns to Vulcan's liquid-fueled core stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, though that does not establish an engine fault. Fuel delivery or another first-stage system could also be responsible, and the investigation is ongoing.

According to recent reports, the BE-4 also powers Blue Origin's Latest Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad during a ground test in May. In August, Blue Origin boss Dave Limp said that the concern originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines. Modifications were made to deal with the problem.

The upper stage's apparently normal performance may offer some reassurance to NASA, although the investigation remains at an early stage. The agency dropped the delayed Exploration Upper Stage earlier this year and is pursuing a stretched Centaur V alongside its existing interim cryogenic propulsion stage as options for Artemis IV.

NASA is targeting Artemis IV for early 2028 and Artemis V for later that year.

ULA mentioned: "We truly understand the impact this has on our customers and are committed to returning to flight as safely and quickly as we can.".

The failure also dents ULA's otherwise impressive launch record. A predecessor of Vulcan, the Atlas V, has a 100 percent success record for payloads reaching orbit. However, it uses Russian RD-180 engines, a dependency the US wishes to remove. ®.

Updated at 1747 GMT to reflect ULA's statement about the likely cause of the failure.

Java4Shell is a reason to use Java

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mccue

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we're less than a day into dealing with "Java4Shell", an issue stemming from how the Java Virtual Machine intrinsifies Base64 encoding code.
  • Industry observers note that this is just one in a string of high profile outages and vulnerabilities.
  • Vulnerabilities tend to be bigger problems when they stem from native code, and they tend to be widespread problems when they come from dependencies many people share.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we're less than a day into dealing with "Java4Shell", an issue stemming from how the Java Virtual Machine intrinsifies Base64 encoding code. If you have a Java deployment you haven't updated yet, add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to the VM flags. Then upgrade your VM to a version where the issue is patched when you can.

Industry observers note that this is just one in a string of high profile outages and vulnerabilities. AI is a good fuzzer, people are finding latent problems with much lower effort than the past. People are pretty worried about this because we're all pretty sure there are more latent problems to find.

Vulnerabilities tend to be bigger problems when they stem from native code, and they tend to be widespread problems when they come from dependencies many people share.

Recent findings suggest that java4Shell is both of these things. A lot of people use Java and the problem stems from a handwritten assembly intrinsic. Fun times.

It has been revealed that but, for a moment, lets say we trust the VM. It is a significant dependency, but it is only one dependency. We can all agree to audit it more closely, reduce the amount of native code in it, proactively run AIs against it, etc. Of course.

Normal Java programs are memory safe. If you use a library which wants to call native code you will get a warning, later a hard error, unless you the person using the library adds --enable-native-access=the.specific.library to their command-line options. This means even with a sprawling dependency tree, which is a problem for all programming language ecosystems, you can know your exact exposure to native code and what dependencies you need to audit more closely.

It has been revealed that compare that to C#, which lets any dependency write assembly inline. Python, JavaScript, Go - everything speaks C and lets any one of your dependencies bring along native code. As we are all learning the hard way, this carries risk.

It has been revealed that not only are Java programs memory safe. They are also fast. The exact mechanism which caused Java4Shell (the ability for the VM to swap out normal Java code for native code) combined with JIT compilation can make the actual performance of a Java program competitive with C. Sometimes a Java program can even be faster. A JIT compiler knows what code paths are actually taken and can optimize around them. They can even refocus what is optimized if the workload changes. It is pretty cool!

Somewhat recently I went through the raytracing in a weekend book with Java.

Benchmarks can be problematic, I know. What I want you to take away is that the JVM makes your code fast enough that most people don't need native code. Unlike, to take a potshot, CPython. There everything is slow as molasses unless you make it a native extension.

So if you are worried AI is going to find security problems with your code, use Java. The problems are likely to be less severe.

Or use Kotlin, Clojure, JRuby, etc. Whatever. Most of what I talked about applies to all of them. Its only what I didn't talk about (the module system) that is Java specific.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chenghengwei revealed on November 19, 2026, that it had recently completed a Series A of nearly RMB 200 million.
  • The proceeds are designated mainly for daily operations and business expansion, specifically supporting scaled mass production and market delivery of its edge AI system-on-chip (SoC) products.
  • Chenghengwei describes CICC Capital as a large state-owned private-equity investor and CRRC Capital as a large state-owned industrial investor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chenghengwei revealed on November 19, 2026, that it had recently completed a Series A of nearly RMB 200 million. CICC Capital, CRRC Capital, Addor Capital, Xichuang Xingwu and Qi’an Investment participated in the financing for the edge AI chip developer.

The proceeds are designated mainly for daily operations and business expansion, specifically supporting scaled mass production and market delivery of its edge AI system-on-chip (SoC) products. The flagship CH37 series has entered small-batch delivery and is intended to supply compute for robots, drones, edge-computing terminals and smart interactive terminals.

Chenghengwei describes CICC Capital as a large state-owned private-equity investor and CRRC Capital as a large state-owned industrial investor. Xichuang Xingwu represents Wuxi local capital, Qi’an Investment is private industrial capital, and Addor Capital is a market-oriented investment institution active in Jiangsu’s semiconductor sector.

In a recent development, the company expects the mix of backers to provide resources for production delivery, customer introductions and ecosystem development. Alongside the upcoming capital, that support is intended to connect the production ramp with customer adoption and the development of a partner base around CH37.

The CH37 series combines an eight-core CPU, 2D and 3D GPUs, a six-core neural processing unit (NPU), a GPGPU for general-purpose computing and image signal processors on a single chip. Chenghengwei says this integration is intended to replace conventional multi-chip designs, reducing power consumption and system complexity while increasing data throughput.

The CH37 product page lists peak AI compute of 64 trillion operations per second (TOPS) using INT8, or 8-bit integer, calculations, with support for FP16, FP32 and FP64 mixed-precision computation. Its six NPU cores are separately rated at up to 48 TOPS, a subsystem figure rather than a second rating for the whole series. The GPGPU provides up to 1 TFLOPS at FP32 and supports CUDA general-purpose computing.

According to recent reports, the product page also lists two independent image-signal-processor channels for visible-light and infrared inputs, plus 4K video encoding and decoding at 120 frames per second. Its AI software supports ONNX models, PyTorch, TensorFlow, ONNX Runtime and an end-to-end NPU deployment toolchain, with CNN, DNN, RNN and Transformer model deployment.

Another critical PHP security release has dropped

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At least one dangerous RCE bug gota fix on Thursday.
  • It has been revealed that apologies in advance to all patch managers and security teams that thought they might get a break this week.
  • These fortunately were not leaked leaked like last month’s critical PHP2Shell flaws – but a Wednesday advisory warned, “The problems rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups,” urging PHP customers to “prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At least one dangerous RCE bug gota fix on Thursday.

It has been revealed that apologies in advance to all patch managers and security teams that thought they might get a break this week. The PHP Foundation has released several more patches, covering all supported versions, and including at least one rated “critical.” including at least one rated "critical.".

These fortunately were not leaked leaked like last month’s critical PHP2Shell flaws – but a Wednesday advisory warned, “The problems rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups,” urging PHP customers to “prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.”.

One of the vulnerabilities is another remote code execution (RCE) flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115560.

In October, the PHP Foundation told The Register that it had reserved this CVE identifier for another RCE bug, but added it would not get an emergency fix like the earlier two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities because the third one doesn't pose the same risk.

CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register at the time. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.”.

The earlier informational advisory urged users to “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.”.

These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().”.

Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled, which the PHP Foundation mentioned is very unlikely in real-world applications.

Overall, a large number of bugs were fixed and CVEs patched across five releases. Get more info on the PHP news page here.

The November security releases follow a hectic October emergency PHP patch-a-thon, with security teams racing to apply fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell, before attackers could abuse the memory-safety flaws in the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites.

While it took miscreants longer to reverse engineer the PHP2Shell fixes than some researchers had anticipated – and the entire internet didn’t burn down in the meantime – the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) did add the two PHP vulns to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26.

Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, as early as October 23, according to Dream researchers.

The Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said the attackers targeted organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks. ®.

Weâre announcing, and honestly celebrating, the next chapter in our push for memory safety: Sovereign Tech Agency have selected us as their partner for helping critical free and open source (FOSS) projects transition to memory safe tech like Rust, as part of their Sovereign Tech Resilience Program. According to recent reports, weâre announcing, and honestly celebrating, the next chapter in our push for memory safety: Sovereign Tech Agency have selected us as their partner for helping critical free and open source (FOSS) projects transition to memory safe tech like Rust, as part of their Sovereign Tech Resilience Program. In this article, weâll go over the Program, why now is the right time to transition, and weâll explain the basics of how FOSS projects can benefit from this collaboration, free of charge.

Industry observers note that the Sovereign Tech Agency are well-known in the FOSS ecosystem for their Sovereign Tech Fund, which does âstrategic investments in the digital infrastructure of our economy and societyâ. In September 2026, they relaunched the Sovereign Tech Resilience Program, which works a little differently; STA has contracted suppliers to perform various services for FOSS projects, to strengthen the resilience of these projects. Unlike many grant programs in the industry, the Sovereign Tech Resilience Program does not give money directly to projects; instead it provides support from a paid-for engineering team.So how does this program strengthen the resilience of FOSS projects? By âimproving projectsâ underlying capacity to prevent, withstand, and respond to [bugs]â in various ways (which you can read more about here), including by offering support for transitioning code bases to Rust, Go, or Python.Transition to memory safetyThat is where we come in. Weâve been contracted to support participating projects in transitioning codebases, whole or in part, from memory-unsafe languages such as C or C++ to memory-safe alternatives where appropriate.The services we will be delivering to FOSS projects are:assessing which components are suitable for rewritesproducing prioritized migration roadmapscarrying out rewrites while maintaining functional equivalence and compatibilitytraining maintainers to keep developing the memory-safe componentsWhy nowA lot of our world depends on various critical open source projects. By now, itâs obvious that hardening these critical open source components, by investing in them and contributing to them, is notable. As weâre right now seeing a surge in both (agentic) cyber attacks and AI-assisted vulnerability discoveries, this has become more pressing than ever before, and weâre not expecting this urgency to let up.There are, thankfully, different ways to go about it, and many excellent initiatives (e.g. the Alpha Omega project), but hereâs why weâre so excited to be a part of this one specifically:The Programsâs criteria ensure a risk and impact based investmentA projectâs maintainers stay in the leadThe effort is substantial enough (i.e. secured for at least 3 years) to create real and lasting impactTo us, being STAâs partner in this also presents a very tangible step in our advocacy for memory safety, which started in 2023 but has felt more pertinent each year since.How to apply for this programFor FOSS projects that are interested, the process is very straightforward:Read the participation criteriaApply to the programGet selectedMake a blueprint with STA and us, while you stay in the leadWe collaboratively execute the planYou can apply for one or multiple areas of support (aside from memory safety, think e.g. software supply chain security, security audits, and more). The resulting engagement can be large or small, long or short, depending on the services youâre interested in and that fit your projectâs needs.Questions?We are currently working on several FOSS projects that are unrelated to the Resilience Program. If youâd like to know more about our open-source work first, here are some of those projects:e-KS and Abacus, for the Dutch Electoral CouncilOpen Device Partnership for MicrosoftVarious projects at Trifecta Tech Foundation, the non-profit that we founded in 2024 to develop and maintain digital commons, open-source software and open standards for the Internet and other vital systems. Projects range from time synchronization (e.g. ntpd-rs and sectime.org), to compression (e.g. zlib-rs) and privilege boundary (e.g. sudo-rs).Any other questions? Please refer to the Programâs FAQ, or reach out to me, Hugo.Weâre thankful for the opportunity to work with various open source projects and maintainers in such a constructive way in the years to come. We look forward to working with you, to helping you get things done that were challenging before, and making a positive impact together!

NVIDIA announced an expanded AI collaboration with Microsoft on November 19, 2026, at Microsoft Ignite, spanning Vera Rubin NVL72 systems running in Azure data centers, broader Nemotron open-model support in Microsoft Foundry, and deployment options for on-premises systems, industrial edge devices and Windows Cloud PCs.

The companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by Vera Rubin NVL72 through Azure’s Vera Rubin preview. The systems are designed for reasoning and agentic applications as well as large-scale model training and inference, connecting the preview to both model development and deployment.

According to recent reports, beyond compute capacity, Microsoft and NVIDIA are working to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure for proprietary and regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys, with work under way to extend those protections across interconnected AI factory infrastructure. The companies are also collaborating on power efficiency through NVIDIA MaxLPS to help data centers obtain more performance from available power.

Microsoft is using NVIDIA technology in its own operations as well. Microsoft AI uses Dynamo for reinforcement-learning rollout inference during post-training, the computationally intensive process that generates experiences used to improve models. Dynamo coordinates inference across a large GPU fleet, optimizing performance and helping manage requests, model updates and recovery from failures in a deployment built on joint Microsoft AI and NVIDIA engineering. Microsoft also uses RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models.

Industry observers note that for enterprise developers, Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering provides control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, connecting model adaptation with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services.

Sources indicate that NVIDIA reported that EY used Programmed Training to adapt Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records. The reported results were a 55% accuracy improvement on EY’s evaluation dataset and a 15x cost reduction compared with proprietary frontier models, providing a measured example of customization for a specialized business task.

The expanded Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute includes Super for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, and Lightning for applications requiring fast responses and tool use. Embed and Rerank support information retrieval, Parse extracts structured information from documents, and Content Safety detects harmful content. NVIDIA listed Bolt for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning and Transcribe for speech recognition as coming soon.

Sources indicate that expanded Nemotron support in Foundry Local brings reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments, while retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables. NVIDIA said Azure Local will support RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners for on-premises AI deployments.

Azure Local is also expanding to Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin for industrial uses including machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations, with Cosmos physical AI models being brought to Foundry Local. These additions extend the collaboration from centralized cloud infrastructure toward systems located closer to the data generated by industrial operations.

NVIDIA said the companies will demonstrate local large-language-model experiences on RTX Spark-powered Windows PCs at Ignite. For GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs, Direct Stream supports up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second with low latency over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027.

NVIDIA’s BioNeMo Agent Toolkit and ALCHEMI Toolkit are also expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog, adding models for life sciences, drug discovery, materials science and chemical science to Microsoft’s agentic research platform. BioNeMo Agent Toolkit lets researchers use natural language to run computational-biology workflows, with agents coordinating the necessary tools and model calls.

Recent findings suggest that the collaboration consequently covers both the supply and use of AI computing: Microsoft is running NVIDIA technology inside its own model development and search operations while offering related infrastructure and model services to enterprises. The announced rollout is staged across systems already running in Azure, a limited Direct Stream preview open for sign-ups and additional models still to come.

European Commission scrambles to contain AI-assisted cyberattack

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Staff HR and medical reimbursement systems taken offline as officials investigate whether personal data was compromised.
  • The European Commission is picking up the pieces after hackers wielding an AI-powered security testing tool targeted its internal IT systems, potentially exposing staff members' personal data.
  • The attack, first reported by Politico, has caused more than 10 days of disruption at the EU's executive arm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Staff HR and medical reimbursement systems taken offline as officials investigate whether personal data was compromised.

The European Commission is picking up the pieces after hackers wielding an AI-powered security testing tool targeted its internal IT systems, potentially exposing staff members' personal data.

The attack, first reported by Politico, has caused more than 10 days of disruption at the EU's executive arm. Among the applications temporarily taken offline were Sysper, which staff use to access payslips, submit timesheets, and request vacation time, and MyPMO, which handles medical reimbursements.

Both were brought back online earlier this week, though Sysper fell over again on Wednesday. The Commission's translation services were also affected.

"The European Commission has taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign," Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told Politico. "Individual systems were targeted and, in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned.".

According to Politico's sources, the Commission's cybersecurity defenders detected hackers using ARTEX, a publicly available AI-powered penetration testing framework. The incident prompted an emergency meeting of the Commission's Corporate Management Board earlier this month, and tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed her fellow commissioners on Wednesday.

The Commission has yet to respond to The Register's questions about the attack, including whether the crooks got their hands on employee data or whether the applications were simply taken offline as a precaution.

Recent findings suggest that the attack might not come as much of a surprise to the Commission's own security bods. CERT-EU, which looks after the cybersecurity of EU institutions, warned on November 5 that it had spotted what it believed to be ARTEX-assisted attacks against organizations under its watch.

According to recent reports, the developer behind ARTEX pulled the project's GitHub repository in October after reports that hackers were putting the software to use. But by then, the code was out in the wild, and anyone wanting to have a crack at an organization's IT estate could get hold of one of several forks.

Recent findings suggest that the FBI also sounded the alarm last week [PDF], revealing that researchers had found more than 1,600 ARTEX consoles exposed to the internet. In some of the attacks detailed by the Feds, hackers went from identifying a target to obtaining privileged access in less than three hours.

“What used to take a skilled operator days or weeks of chaining is now happening in hours because frameworks like ARTEX let a single actor stand up fleets of agents that plan, probe, exploit, and move laterally with almost no further human input after the initial goal is set,” Snehal Antani, CEO of security firm Horizon3.ai, told The Register.

Antani stated the proliferation of these tools could also make life harder for investigators trying to establish who's behind an attack, as government-backed hackers and garden-variety cybercriminals increasingly draw from the same toolbox.

It has been revealed that commission staff at least appear to have been paid on time. According to Politico, some couldn't book time off or submit their timesheets, but salaries landed as usual. Whether the hackers managed to snoop on their payslips is something the Commission has yet to establish. ®.

Make your ZeroGPU Spaces go brrr with ahead-of-time compilation

📅 02 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that zeroGPU lets anyone spin up powerful Nvidia H200 hardware in Hugging Face Spaces without keeping a GPU locked for idle traffic.
  • Industry observers note that this is where PyTorch ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation comes in.
  • The result: snappier demos and a smoother experience, with speedups ranging from 1.3×–1.8× on models like Flux, Wan, and LTX 🔥.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that zeroGPU lets anyone spin up powerful Nvidia H200 hardware in Hugging Face Spaces without keeping a GPU locked for idle traffic. It’s efficient, flexible, and ideal for demos but it doesn’t always make full use of everything the GPU and CUDA stack can offer. Generating images or videos can take a significant amount of time. Being able to squeeze out more performance, taking advantage of the H200 hardware, does matter in this case.

Industry observers note that this is where PyTorch ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation comes in. Instead of compiling models on the fly (which doesn’t play nicely with ZeroGPU’s short-lived processes), AoT lets you optimize once and reload instantly.

The result: snappier demos and a smoother experience, with speedups ranging from 1.3×–1.8× on models like Flux, Wan, and LTX 🔥.

In this post, we’ll show how to wire up Ahead-of-Time (AoT) compilation in ZeroGPU Spaces. We'll explore advanced tricks like FP8 quantization and dynamic shapes, and share working demos you can try right away. If you cannot wait, we invite you to check out some ZeroGPU-powered demos on the zerogpu-aoti organization.

Pro users and Team / Enterprise org members can create ZeroGPU Spaces, while anyone can freely use them (Pro, Team and Enterprise users get 8x more ZeroGPU quota).

Spaces is a platform powered by Hugging Face that allows ML practitioners to easily publish demo apps.

Typical demo apps on Spaces look like:.

This works great, but ends up reserving a GPU for the Space during its entire lifetime – even when it has no user activity.

When executing .to('cuda') on this line:.

It has been revealed that pyTorch initializes the NVIDIA driver, which sets up the process on CUDA forever. This is not very resource-efficient given that app traffic is not perfectly smooth, but is rather extremely sparse and spiky.

ZeroGPU takes a just-in-time approach to GPU initialization. Instead of setting up the main process on CUDA, it automatically forks the process, sets it up on CUDA, runs the GPU tasks, and finally kills the fork when the GPU needs to be released.

Thanks to the Python spaces package, the only code change needed to get this behaviour is as follows:.

By importing spaces and adding the @spaces.GPU decorator, we:.

ZeroGPU right now allocates an MIG slice of H200 (3g.71gb profile). Additional MIG sizes including full slice (7g.141gb profile) will come in late 2025.

Sources indicate that modern ML frameworks like PyTorch and JAX have the concept of compilation that can be used to optimize model latency or inference time. Behind the scenes, compilation applies a series of (often hardware-dependent) optimization steps such as operator fusion, constant folding, etc.

PyTorch (from 2.0 onwards) currently has two major interfaces for compilation:.

torch.compile works great in standard environments: it compiles your model the first time it runs, and reuses the optimized version for subsequent calls.

Industry observers note that however, on ZeroGPU, given that the process is freshly spun up for (almost) every GPU task, it means that torch.compile can’t efficiently re-use compilation and is thus forced to rely on its filesystem cache to restore compiled models. Depending on the model being compiled, this process takes from a few dozen seconds to a couple of minutes, which is way too much for practical GPU tasks in Spaces.

This is where ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation shines.

Recent findings suggest that with AoT, we can export a compiled model once, save it, and later reload it instantly in any process, which is exactly what we need for ZeroGPU. This helps us reduce framework overhead and also eliminates cold-start timings typically incurred in just-in-time compilation.

According to recent reports, but how can we do ahead-of-time compilation on ZeroGPU? Let’s dive in.

Let's go back to our ZeroGPU base example and unpack what we need to enable AoT compilation. For the purpose of this demo, we will use the black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev model:.

In the discussion below, we only compile the transformer component of pipe since, in these generative models, the transformer (or more generally, the denoiser) is the most computationally heavy component.

Compiling a model ahead-of-time with PyTorch involves multiple steps:.

It has been revealed that recall that we’re going to compile the model ahead of time. Therefore, we need to derive example inputs for the model. Note that these are the same kinds of inputs we expect to see during the actual runs. To capture those inputs, we will leverage the spaces.aoti_capture helper from the spaces package:.

When used as a context manager, aoti_capture intercepts the call to any callable (pipe.transformer in our case), prevents it from executing, captures the input arguments that would have been passed to it, and stores their values in call.args and call.kwargs.

Now that we have example args and kwargs for our transformer component, we can export it to a PyTorch ExportedProgram by using torch.export.export utility:.

An exported PyTorch program is a computation graph that represents the tensor computations along with the original model parameter values.

Once the model is exported, compiling it is pretty straightforward.

A traditional AoT compilation in PyTorch often requires saving the model on disk so it can be later reloaded. In our case, we’ll leverage a helper function part of the spaces package: spaces.aoti_compile. It's a tiny wrapper around torch._inductor.aot_compile that manages saving and lazy-loading the model as needed. It's meant to be used like this:.

This compiled_transformer is now an AoT-compiled binary ready to be used for inference.

Now we need to bind our compiled transformer to our original pipeline, i.e., the pipeline.

Industry observers note that A naive and almost working approach is to simply patch our pipeline like pipe.transformer = compiled_transformer. Unfortunately, this approach does not work because it deletes vital attributes like dtype, config, etc. Only patching the forward method does not work well either because we are then keeping original model parameters in memory, often leading to OOM errors at runtime.

spaces package provides a utility for this, too -- spaces.aoti_apply:.

Et voilà! It will take care of patching pipe.transformer.forward with our compiled model, as well as cleaning old model parameters out of memory.

To perform the first three steps (intercepting input examples, exporting the model, and compiling it with PyTorch inductor), we need a real GPU. CUDA emulation that you get outside of @spaces.GPU function is not enough because compilation is truly hardware-dependent, for instance, relying on micro-benchmark runs to tune the generated code. This is why we need to wrap it all inside a @spaces.GPU function and then get our compiled model back to the root of our app. Starting from our original demo code, this gives:.

With just a dozen lines of additional code, we’ve successfully made our demo quite faster (1.7x faster in the case of FLUX.1-dev).

If you want to learn more about AoT compilation, you can read PyTorch's AOTInductor tutorial.

Now that we have demonstrated the speedups one can realize under the constraints of operating with ZeroGPUs, we will discuss a few gotchas that came up while working with this setup.

According to recent reports, aoT can be combined with quantization to deliver even greater speedups. For image and video generation, the FP8 post-training dynamic quantization schemes deliver good speed-quality trade-offs. However, FP8 requires a CUDA compute capability of at least 9.0 to work. Thankfully, for ZeroGPUs, since they’re based on H200s, we can already take advantage of the FP8 quantization schemes.

To enable FP8 quantization within our AoT compilation workflow, we can leverage the APIs provided by torchao like so:.

(You can find more details about TorchAO here.).

Images and videos can come in different shapes and sizes. Hence, it’s key to also account for shape dynamism when performing AoT compilation. The primitives provided by torch.export.export make it easily configurable to provide what inputs should be treated accordingly for dynamic shapes, as shown below.

For the case of Flux.1-Dev transformer, changes in different image resolutions will affect two of its forward arguments:.

It has been revealed that we start by defining a range in which we want to let the (latent) image resolutions vary. To derive these value ranges, we inspected the shapes of hidden_states in the pipeline with respect to varied image resolutions. The exact values are model-dependent and require manual inspection and some intuition. For Flux.1-Dev, we ended up with:.

We then define a map of argument names and which dimensions in their input values we expect to be dynamic:.

In a recent development, then we need to make our dynamic shapes object replicate the structure of our example inputs. The inputs that do not need dynamic shapes must be set to None. This can be done very easily with PyTorch tree_map utility:.

Now, when performing the export step, we simply supply transformer_dynamic_shapes to torch.export.export:.

Check out this Space that shows how to use both quantization and dynamic shapes during the export step.

Dynamic shapes is sometimes not enough when dynamism is too important.

This is, for instance, the case with the Wan family of video generation models if you want your compiled model to generate different resolutions. One thing can be done in this case: compile one model per resolution while keeping the model parameters shared and dispatching the right one at runtime.

Industry observers note that here is a minimal example of this approach: zerogpu-aoti-multi.py. You can also see a fully working implementation of this paradigm in the Wan 2.2 Space.

Industry observers note that since the ZeroGPU hardware and CUDA drivers are perfectly compatible with Flash-Attention 3 (FA3), we can use it in our ZeroGPU Spaces to speed things up even further. FA3 works with ahead-of-time compilation. So, this is ideal for our case.

Compiling and building FA3 from source can take several minutes, and this process is hardware-dependent. As people, we wouldn’t want to lose precious ZeroGPU compute hours. This is where Hugging Face kernels library comes to the rescue. It provides access to pre-built kernels that are compatible for a given hardware. For example, when we try to run:.

It tries to load a kernel from the kernels-community/vllm-flash-attn3 repository, which is compatible with the current setup. Otherwise, it will error out due to incompatibility issues. Luckily for us, this works seamlessly on the ZeroGPU Spaces. This means we can leverage the power of FA3 on ZeroGPU, using the kernels library.

Here is a fully working example of an FA3 attention processor for the Qwen-Image model.

According to recent reports, so far, we have been compiling the full model. Depending on the model, full model compilation can lead to significantly long cold start times. Long cold start times make the development experience unpleasant.

We can also choose to compile regions within a model, significantly reducing the cold start times, while retaining almost all the benefits of full model compilation. Regional compilation becomes promising when a model has repeated blocks of computation. A standard language model, for example, has a number of identically structured Transformer blocks.

According to recent reports, in our example, we can compile the repeated blocks of the Flux transformer ahead of time, and propagate the compiled graph to the remaining repeated blocks. The Flux Transformer has two kinds of repeated blocks: FluxTransformerBlock and FluxSingleTransformerBlock.

You can check out this Space for a complete example.

💡 For Flux.1-Dev, switching to regional compilation reduces the compilation time from 6 minutes to just 30 seconds while delivering identical speedups.

According to recent reports, once a model (or even a model block) is compiled ahead of time, we can serialize the compiled graph module as an artifact and reuse later. In the context of a ZeroGPU-powered demo on Spaces, this will significantly cut down the demo startup time by skipping the compilation time.

To keep the storage light, we can just save the compiled model graph without including any model parameters inside the artifact.

Check out this collection that reveals a full workflow of obtaining compiled model graph, pushing it to the Hub, and then using it to build a demo.

In a recent development, zeroGPU within Hugging Face Spaces is a powerful feature that enables AI builders by providing access to powerful compute. In this post, we demonstrated how people can benefit from PyTorch’s ahead-of-time compilation techniques to speed up their applications that leverage ZeroGPU.

Sources indicate that we demonstrate speedups with Flux.1-Dev, but these techniques are not limited to just this model. Therefore, we encourage you to give these techniques a try and provide us with feedback in this community discussion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Norwegian energy giant Equinor says oil and gas production remains unaffected.

Norwegian energy giant Equinor is battling a cyberattack on its IT systems, though the organization insists that hackers haven't disrupted its oil and gas production.

Equinor, Europe's largest supplier of natural gas, first disclosed the attack on Tuesday evening, saying it had called in the relevant resources to deal with the intrusion and had found no indication that any data had been stolen.

In an update on Wednesday, the company remarked it had a better handle on how the attack was carried out and which of its systems had been compromised, though it stopped short of sharing either of those details.

Recent findings suggest that "As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading," Equinor said. The organization added that it had found nothing to suggest the incident would affect employees, partners, or suppliers.

In a recent development, in a further enhancement on Thursday, Equinor noted the attack remained ongoing but did not appear to be specifically targeting the organization. Production continued normally, with no indications that data had been stolen or altered. The incident has been reported to police.

It has been revealed that what kind of attack Equinor is dealing with remains a mystery. The tech giant hasn't identified those responsible, disclosed whether it's received any demands from the hackers, or stated when it expects the affected systems to be fully restored.

The Register has asked Equinor to elaborate, including whether any of its UK operations have been affected and whether the hackers managed to venture beyond its corporate IT network.

Sources indicate that equinor spokesperson Ellen Maria Skjelsbæk told Norwegian news agency NTB that the firm hadn't lost access to its IT systems, though staff could have trouble accessing some corporate applications and services. Email appears to be among the casualties, with Reuters reporting that the company's internal email system was down.

It has been revealed that equinor, which traded as Statoil until 2018, is still largely in the hands of the Norwegian state, which owns 67 percent of the tech giant. The oil and gas biz employs around 25,000 people and operates in more than 20 countries.

The bulk of Equinor's oil and gas production takes place off the coast of Norway, but the company also pumps oil and gas in the UK, US, Brazil, and Canada. It's one of the companies behind Dogger Bank, the enormous offshore wind project off England's northeast coast, and is also in the business of capturing and storing carbon dioxide.

Equinor's assurances about production will be particularly welcome in Europe, which has become increasingly reliant on Norwegian gas since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The attack comes just weeks after Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) raised its cyberattack risk assessment to four on a five-point scale. The agency said the number of successful cyber operations against Norwegian businesses had tripled over the preceding six months and warned of potential disruption to essential services, including water and electricity supplies.

Sources indicate that europe has already had a few nasty reminders this year of what happens when hackers get their hands on industrial equipment. Last week, the French government pinned a series of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems at more than 700 retail sites in October on a hacking unit affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The crooks turned up the temperature in supermarket fridges and freezers, ruining tens of millions of euros' worth of food and starting fires at some premises.

Nothing suggests Equinor's hackers have similar ambitions, or that they've got anywhere near the kit used to extract and transport oil and gas. Given how much of Europe depends on that kit continuing to work, a little more detail from the Norwegian energy giant wouldn't go amiss. ®.

Industry News: SAIR: Accelerating Pharma R&D with AI-Powered Structural Intelligence

📅 02 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This summer, SandboxAQ released the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR), the largest dataset of co-folded 3D protein-ligand structures paired with experimentally measured IC₅₀ labels, directly linking molecular structure to drug potency and overcoming a longstanding scarcity in training data.
  • In a recent development, SAIR is an open-sourced dataset and is publicly available for free under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license, making it immediately actionable for commercial and non-commercial R&D pipelines.
  • In a recent development, AI and computer-aided design have great potential in dramatically accelerating the development of new drugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This summer, SandboxAQ released the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR), the largest dataset of co-folded 3D protein-ligand structures paired with experimentally measured IC₅₀ labels, directly linking molecular structure to drug potency and overcoming a longstanding scarcity in training data. This dataset is now available on Hugging Face, and for the first time, researchers have open access to more than 5 million AI‑generated, high‑accuracy protein-ligand 3D structures, each paired with validated empirical binding potency data.

In a recent development, SAIR is an open-sourced dataset and is publicly available for free under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license, making it immediately actionable for commercial and non-commercial R&D pipelines. More than just a dataset, SAIR is a strategic asset that bridges the long-standing data gap in AI-powered drug design. It empowers pharmaceutical, biotech, and tech‑bio leaders to accelerate R&D, expand target horizons, and supercharge AI models – moving more of the costly, lengthy drug design and optimization from the wet lab to in silico. This means shorter hit‑to‑lead timelines, more efficient lead optimization, fewer dead‑end projects, and a more predictable path from initial idea to clinical candidate.

In a recent development, AI and computer-aided design have great potential in dramatically accelerating the development of new drugs. For decades, scientists have dreamed about AI that could identify or design a potent, non-toxic, and efficacious compound from a prompt describing the disease pathway, practically compressing years of drug R&D into a few minutes on a computer. However, this vision is bottlenecked by AI's ability to predict critical drug properties like potency, toxicity, etc., based solely on its molecular structure.

Furthermore, traditional structure‑based discovery is often slowed early by the determination of reliable 3D structures. Three‑dimensional molecular structure dictates a molecule’s functionality, dynamics and interactions, which is especially important when a potential drug candidate is expected to bind to a human protein target.

Experimental methods, such as X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, require extensive time and investment, and many promising disease targets still lack experimentally validated structural information. Computer simulations have helped lower the barrier of getting 3D structures and predicting binding affinity. However, earlier generations of algorithms for protein folding and docking (like AlphaFold and Vina respectively) only predict static snapshots of molecules and proteins (which, in reality, are inherently dynamic and shape-changing).

SAIR solves that constraint by compiling over 1 million unique computationally co-folded protein–ligand pairs, ultimately yielding 5.24 million distinct 3D complexes (five different co-folded structures per pair). Each structure is paired with a curated IC₅₀ measurement from ChEMBL or BindingDB, providing for the first time a scalable link between high-quality 3D structures and drug potency, and bridging the historic data gap that has hindered AI-driven discovery. Deep-learned affinity models such as Boltz-2, trained on similar data, have been shown to yield up to a 1,000x speed-up over the traditional, first-principle approach.

Recent findings suggest that creating SAIR was a major feat of high-performance AI computing. It took more than 130,000 GPU hours to compute the SAIR dataset using Boltz1, a cofolding AI model, on a cluster of 760 NVIDIA H100 processors, leveraging the NVIDIA DGX Cloud through Google Cloud Platform.

Capturing highly granular node, operator, scheduler, and GPU metrics, as well as a close collaboration on both infrastructure and workload optimization, helped NVIDIA AI Accelerator and SandboxAQ engineering teams identify bottlenecks and optimize configurations to achieve the highest workload throughput.

Recent findings suggest that consequently, the two teams were able to achieve > 95% GPU compute utilization for generating the SAIR dataset. This enabled us to create SAIR in three weeks – as opposed to the original estimate of three months (more than a 4X speed up) – and resulted in a highly optimized, GPU-native computational workflow that seamlessly integrates with today’s cutting-edge enterprise compute environments.

Recent findings suggest that generating such a massive volume of data is only half the story. Equally important is confidence in its quality, which is why every predicted complex underwent rigorous validation with PoseBusters, an industry-standard, open-source tool for benchmarking structure-related AI in drug discovery. This tool checks chemical sanity and physical plausibility.

The end result was that 97 percent of SAIR’s structures passed all checks. In addition to PoseBusters validation, we benchmarked leading affinity prediction methods, such as empirical scoring functions, 3D CNNs, and graph neural networks, across SAIR’s synthetic structures and experimental IC₅₀ values. The detailed results of these studies are available in our scientific manuscript on bioRxiv.

SAIR data is a reliable foundation for benchmarking new models as well as downstream modelling, screening, and design.

Industry observers note that A persistent challenge in drug discovery is the “dark proteome,” or disease‑relevant proteins for which experimental structures simply do not exist. SAIR illuminates these uncharted regions by providing credible, AI‑predicted complexes wherever experimental data is scarce. For example, more than 40 percent of the proteins in the SAIR dataset have no available structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) whatsoever, with or without a ligand. SAIR addresses one of the biggest challenges with existing AI models, low generalizability due to data scarcity. With SAIR, scientists can now explore targets that were previously deemed undruggable, armed with structural hypotheses to guide virtual screening and lead optimization using trustworthy model predictions.

Industry observers note that moreover, SAIR’s cross‑target breadth uncovers polypharmacology patterns and elucidates how a single molecule might interact with multiple proteins. Leveraging this rich tapestry of interactions, you can train AI models to predict off‑target effects or identify fresh repurposing opportunities, equipping your organization with a deeper understanding of compound profiles before any lab work begins.

SAIR is freely available on Hugging Face. Here’s a quick guide to pull SAIR from Hugging Face, peek at the main table, and (optionally) download a few structure archives.

We use the Hub to fetch files and pandas+pyarrow to read the Parquet.

Industry observers note that structure files are shipped as many .tar.gz archives under structures_compressed/. List them and pick what you need.

Industry observers note that each archive can be large (≈10 GB). Download only the ones you need and extract them locally.

A full version of this script, including more robust logging and validation, is available in the README file for your convenience. For more details, visit the SAIR homepage, read our manuscript on bioRxiv, or watch our 25-minute joint webinar with NVIDIA, where we demonstrate SAIR and explain how data is structured within it. Extensive documentation, tutorials, and example benchmarks are available to facilitate its use and accelerate internal adoption.The future of drug discovery is data-driven, AI-accelerated, and grounded in scalable, high-quality structural insights. While we don’t yet have AI that can design effective drug therapies with just a prompt, SAIR brings researchers ever closer to that goal with new data and insights that can potentially shave years from even AI-accelerated R&D pipelines.We can’t wait to see what researchers will build using SAIR, and SandboxAQ experts are here to support them throughout the discovery process.

Contact the authors or post on the SAIR dataset discussion page.

Authors: Arman Zaribafiyan, Georgia Channing, Zane Beckwith, and Rudi Plesch.

According to recent reports, modern Industrials announced on November 19, 2026 that it raised $6 million in seed funding to expand custom AI agents for manufacturers and distributors. Glasswing Ventures led the round, TMV co-led it, and a16z speedrun and other investors participated.

It has been revealed that chief executive Austin Mao said the capital will accelerate development, expand the team and bring the company’s software approach to more manufacturers and distributors. That approach centers on building agents around each customer’s operations, with the software working inside existing systems.

Industry observers note that modern Industrials is targeting the manual work that connects emails, spreadsheets and business systems in industrial operations. Its agents are designed for sales, procurement, inventory management, operations and customer engagement at industrial and building-materials manufacturers and distributors.

According to recent reports, named applications include quoting, order entry, demand planning, vendor management and customer support. The objective is to automate complex processes and equip teams with better information for decisions while minimizing disruption to existing operations. That makes customer-specific integration a central part of what the latest capital is intended to scale.

Modern Industrials’ product documentation describes a staged path to automation. Systems remain read-only until a customer grants write access, which is scoped to specific approved actions. Customers decide how much work runs autonomously and can revise that choice later.

Recent findings suggest that most customers begin with humans reviewing everything, then allow more automation after the system proves accurate on real order flow, according to the documentation. Across sales, procurement, finance and operations, the agents can answer questions, generate insights, make decisions and execute work.

Recent findings suggest that ERP connectivity supports that deployment model. The tech giant lists integrations with Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics 365, JD Edwards, Acumatica, Epicor Eclipse, Epicor Prophet 21 and Infor, among others. Those connections let customers add agent-driven workflows while retaining the software already used to run their operations.

Sources indicate that the three co-founders combine AI engineering and consulting backgrounds. Mao worked on Fortune 100 AI strategy and implementation projects at McKinsey. Chief technology officer Ankit Bhargava was a member of xAI’s technical staff and previously an Uber engineer, while chief product officer Vatsal Bhargava was a machine-learning engineer at Google. Other founding-team members have experience at Palantir, Meta and J.P. Morgan.

Steve Rask, CEO of private equity group AC Summit and MJB Wood Group, forecast that the technology “will save hundreds of hours and millions of dollars.” MJB, a sales, sourcing and manufacturing partner in the wood-products supply chain, is now expanding Modern Industrials to other portfolio companies.

John Chisholm, president of Atlantic Forest Products, noted Modern Industrials had found a way to solve each upcoming challenge his team presented. Together, the customer accounts provide early examples of the tailored deployments the company plans to expand.

Sources indicate that glasswing founder and managing partner Rudina Seseri said advances in reasoning and agentic AI could unlock efficiencies that traditional software could not address, with the potential to improve revenue and margins for industrial customers. TMV co-founder and managing partner Soraya Darabi said the founders’ practice of understanding each customer’s business and building around it helped earn customer trust swiftly.

It has been revealed that the seed round gives Modern Industrials resources to broaden that model beyond its early deployments. Its scaling test is whether it can add people and customers while preserving the tailored integrations and graduated, permission-based automation that distinguish its deployment approach.

  • A Russian national is being held in custody after being arrested for allegedly spying on a US defense tech tech giant in Palo Alto, shoulder-surfing employees, and dropping remote surveillance devices at their homes.
  • Igor D'iu was indicted after FBI agents surveilled his activities between June and October 2026, which they say were issued as "tasks" from what is thought to be Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to an affidavit [PDF] signed by an FBI special agent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DoJ claims suspect part of 4-month operation to steal secrets, surveil employees.

A Russian national is being held in custody after being arrested for allegedly spying on a US defense tech tech giant in Palo Alto, shoulder-surfing employees, and dropping remote surveillance devices at their homes.

Igor D'iu was indicted after FBI agents surveilled his activities between June and October 2026, which they say were issued as "tasks" from what is thought to be Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to an affidavit [PDF] signed by an FBI special agent.

After FBI agents secured a warrant to raid D'iu's temporary premises in October, they say that Telegram messages harvested from his seized devices confirmed investigators' findings and revealed that he was spying on an unnamed firm.

Court documents describe the company in question as a large technology and defense company with offices in Palo Alto, and media-reported links to the Russia-Ukraine war.

While unconfirmed officially, the company has widely been reported as Palantir, which did not respond to our request for confirmation.

D'iu allegedly received instructions from Telegram contacts, whom he only suspected were representatives of the Russian government, weeks after entering the US illegally in July.

The indictment alleges he was ordered to surveil employees' homes, take photographs of their screens while working remotely at coffee shops, and permit his handlers to remotely access his laptop for the purpose of capturing data from nearby devices owned by the firm’s employees.

In some cases, the filing alleges, D’iu was asked to leave a laptop outside one employee's apartment complex, all while allowing his Telegram handlers to remotely operate the device.

The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come back to collect it three hours later, the filing claims.

D'iu is also allegedly to have followed two female employees in his rented car, driving dangerously and violating multiple road laws to do so.

One of the two employees was followed briefly, but D'iu followed another for nearly 30 miles, according to the affidavit signed by FBI special agent Winston Wong.

D'iu was noted to have followed the woman as she performed U-turns, illegal left turns, ran red lights, navigated via back and side streets, and through grocery store parking lots.

The car following her only peeled away after the woman drove to the San Francisco Mission police station on the advice of a 911 call handler.

Questioned about the incident, which according to police reports caused the woman significant emotional distress, D'iu confirmed he was the driver but  claimed he was following her to ask her out on a date.

The affidavit did not detail the suspect's background beyond his alleged offenses in the US earlier this year, although it mentioned Russian intelligence's history of recruiting "criminal proxies, organized crime groups, and other disposable agents" to carry out operations.

According to the FBI's account, D'iu entered the US illegally – without relevant visas – in either June or July 2026. Travel records obtained on September 10 indicated that his last recorded journey was from Istanbul to Mexico City. There was no record of him entering the US.

Investigators would later come to know that he travelled on that Istanbul-Mexico City flight on June 7, allegedly using a ticket provided to him by one of the three contacts from whom he received orders via Telegram.

A Facebook account, registered using a Mexican +528 number and D'iu's name, posted on June 30 asking for help getting "closer to Latest York," adding that "I'll pay as much as needed." The account replied to a response from someone who told him to contact a Mexico phone number on WhatsApp.

The filing claims the first mobile phone signals associated with D'iu's devices did not ping US towers until a month later, on July 31, suggesting he did not arrive in the US - specifically McAllen, Texas - until around that date. Telegram messages would also go on to confirm that he was allegedly helped across the border by an "Uzbek contact" in Mexico.

It has been revealed that records obtained from Google showed D'iu created a Google account in April. According to the affidavit, D'iu used it to search for the company's Wikipedia page on July 28, and on August 3, used Google's AI to devise a route around Texas that bypassed border checkpoints.

The FBI believes D'iu's "spying" began in mid-August, after he bought a laptop, a Wi-Fi device, a puck device, and an additional phone. At this point, the agency claims, he had received his first order to visit a coffee shop near the Palo Alto organization’s office and snap employees' laptop screens before sending copies back to his handlers.

Three days later, D'iu was ordered to go back to a coffee shop and allow his Telegram contacts to remotely control the laptop and collect data from employee devices that were in range, claims the filing.

D'iu was paid $15,000 on three occasions between August 12 and October 6, according to the court documents. To verify the transaction, he was told to send a picture of a dollar bill's serial number to the Telegram contacts, along with a description of what he was wearing. A courier would then arrive, confirming the serial number and handing D'iu the cash.

The filing alleges he used this money to purchase the tech equipment, accommodation, and travel, including a rented silver 2026 Lexus RX 350 from a private owner in Los Angeles on August 22, which he is said to have driven back to San Francisco.

The same Lexus was captured on security footage outside the unnamed tech giant's office on September 1, and over the following two days was implicated in the two instances of female employees being followed.

Contacted by Palo Alto police on September 4, D'iu confirmed he was the driver who dangerously followed the female staffer for nearly 30 minutes, but claimed he knew nothing about the nearby businesses. D'iu would then claim he followed the woman because he thought she was beautiful and wanted to ask her out on a date, and denied following anyone else.

According to recent reports, the affidavit goes on to allege that D'iu then traveled to Reno, Nevada, to lay low after his run-in with the police. He spent the time trying to reroute DHL deliveries from San Francisco to his hideout address, which US Customs would later intercept.

These ended up containing fake IDs with the images the DoJ claims matched D'iu's, including Uzbek documents, a US passport whose number belonged to a Fresh York woman, and a social security card registered to a "Hugo Landry Johns.".

He traveled back to the Bay Area in late September, swapping his silver Lexus for a white 2016 Dodge Challenger, and received additional instructions from his handlers, including the order to leave a remote-controlled laptop outside the apartment complex, says the filing.

One Telegram contact named Ian Morales sent photos of at least four employees and their addresses, along with instructions for D'iu to dress as a food delivery worker and visit those locations, asking whoever answered to verify they lived there.

FBI agents executed a search warrant on October 8, seizing a cache of evidence, including what they listed as being:.

A notebook with 10 handwritten addresses supplied by Telegram contacts, along with times the suspect was supposed to attend those locations, at least five of which were for firm employees’ homes.

Profile packages for at least three employees, including: Names, personal information, education and employment histories, names of relatives, narrative histories, and assessments of leadership qualities, strengths, and weaknesses.

Per the affidavit, D'iu was noted to have only become suspicious of the tasks he was being ordered to complete in October, when his handlers ordered the laptop to be dropped near the apartment complex.

"D'iu gradually began to understand he was doing something bad and that his actions were illegal," the affidavit stated.

At this point, he allegedly asked the Telegram contacts who he was working for, to which they replied "the Motherland," and the company he was surveilling was involved in providing weapons to Ukraine, resulting in D’iu suspecting the Russian government.

Wong said in the affidavit: "Based on my training, experience, and research, D'iu's communications with his Telegram contacts is consistent with the tactics of [Russian intelligence] and its criminal proxies for spotting, assessing, recruiting, and handling intelligence assets and sources.

"D'iu's targeting of the firm and its employees is also consistent with [Russian intelligence] objectives in Russia's war against Ukraine.".

The Russian national was indicted and charged with two counts related to spying offences, and one count related to the fake identity documents. He is next due in court on November 24 but remains in federal custody. ®.

Breaking: Welcome EmbeddingGemma, Google's new efficient embedding model

📅 04 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases.
  • Text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent.
  • Sources indicate that building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases. Designed for speed and efficiency, the model features a compact size of 308M parameters and a 2K context window, unlocking upcoming possibilities for mobile RAG pipelines, agents, and more. EmbeddingGemma is trained to support over 100 languages and is the highest-ranking text-only multilingual embedding model under 500M on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) at the time of writing.

Text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent. These vectors enable fast similarity search, clustering, classification, and retrieval across massive corpora, powering everything from recommendation engines and semantic search to retrieval-augmented generation and code‑search tools. Embedding models that calculate these embeddings are widely used, with well over 200 million monthly downloads on Hugging Face.

Sources indicate that building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet. With just 308M parameters, a 2k‑token context window, and support for over 100 languages, EmbeddingGemma delivers state‑of‑the‑art performance on the Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark (MMTEB) while staying under 200 MB of RAM when quantized.

The various design choices result in a very practical, open-source tool for computing high-quality multilingual embeddings on everyday devices.

In this blogpost, we describe the EmbeddingGemma architecture and training, and show you how to use the model with various frameworks like Sentence Transformers, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, txtai, Transformers.js, Text Embedding Inference, and ONNX.

Afterwards, we demonstrate how to finetune EmbeddingGemma on your domain for even stronger performance. In our example, we finetune EmbeddingGemma on the Medical Instruction and Retrieval Dataset (MIRIAD). The resulting model, sentence-transformers/embeddinggemma-300m-medical, achieves state-of-the-art performance on our task: retrieving passages of scientific medical papers in response to detailed medical questions. It even outperforms models twice as big on this task.

Sources indicate that embeddingGemma builds on the Gemma3 transformers backbone, but modified to use bi-directional attention instead of causal (one-way) attention. This means that earlier tokens in the sequence can attend to later tokens, effectively turning the architecture from a decoder into an encoder. Encoder models can outperform LLMs, which are decoders, on embedding tasks like retrieval (Weller et al., 2025). With this backbone, the model can process a sizable 2048 tokens at once, sufficient for typical retrieval inputs, especially given that larger inputs often result in information loss in the text embeddings.

Beyond the latest Gemma3-based encoder backbone, which produces token embeddings, a mean pooling layer converts these token embeddings into text embeddings. Lastly, two dense layers transform the text embeddings into their final form, a 768-dimensional vector.

According to recent reports, the EmbeddingGemma model has been trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), allowing you to truncate the 768‑dimensional output to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions on demand. This results in faster downstream processing and lower memory and disk space utilization. See the Sentence Transformers usage for a snippet showing how to perform this truncation.

It has been revealed that the model has been trained using a carefully curated, multilingual corpus totalling approximately 320 billion tokens. The proprietary dataset is a blend of publicly available web text, code and technical documentation, and synthetic task‑specific examples. It has been filtered to avoid Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM), sensitive data, and low-quality or unsafe content.

It has been revealed that embeddingGemma was benchmarked on the MMTEB (Multilingual, v2) and MTEB (English, v2) suites, which span a wide range of tasks, domains, and languages. Despite its modest 308M‑parameter size, the model consistently beats comparable baselines while keeping a very small memory footprint.

Recent findings suggest that the results will be listed on the official MTEB Leaderboard. We exclude any model that has been trained on more than 20% of the MTEB data, to mitigate potential over‑fitting.

The demo can also be experienced in full screen.

Experience the demo yourself on a Desktop device.

EmbeddingGemma is integrated with many popular tools, making it easy to incorporate into your existing workflows and applications. The model has been integrated in Sentence Transformers, and thus also in projects that use Sentence Transformers behind the scenes, such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and txtai. See the examples below to get started with your preferred framework.

For production deployments, you can use Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) to serve the model efficiently on various hardware configurations, and you can use Transformers.js for use in web applications.

According to recent reports, regardless of your framework choice, you should be mindful of the prompts. For embedding models, prompts are prepended to the input text to allow the model to distinguish between different tasks. EmbeddingGemma was trained with these prompt names and prompts, so they should also be included when using the model:.

Because google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with MRL, the embeddings generated by this model can be truncated to lower dimensionalities without considerably hurting the evaluation performance. Embeddings with lower dimensionalities are both cheaper to store on disk and in memory, as well as faster for downstream tasks like retrieval, clustering, or classification.

In Sentence Transformers, you can set a lower dimensionality using the truncate_dim parameter on either the SentenceTransformer initialization or when calling model.encode/model.encode_query/model.encode_document:.

Note that the ranking is preserved despite using 3x smaller embeddings compared to the full-sized embeddings.
