You can easily deploy EmbeddingGemma for both development and production using Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) version 1.8.1 or later.

If you run the Docker container with the cuda-1.8.1 tag, it includes support for multiple GPU architectures: Turing, Ampere, Ada Lovelace, and Hopper. For a lighter image tailored to just your GPU, you can instead use a specific tag such as turing-1.8.1, 1.8.1 and 86-1.8.1 (Ampere), 89-1.8.1 (Ada Lovelace), or hopper-1.8.1.

Once deployed, regardless of the device or runtime, you can leverage the /v1/embeddings endpoint based on the OpenAI Embeddings API Specification to generate embeddings.

Alternatively, you can also leverage the /embed endpoint from the Text Embeddings Inference Embeddings API, which supports the prompt_name parameter, meaning there’s no need to manually prepend the prompt to the inputs but select it via prompt_name instead.

Additionally, note that since google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), you can also leverage the dimensions parameter, on both /v1/embeddings and /embed, to truncate the embeddings to lower dimensionalities (512, 256, and 128) without hurting the evaluation performance.

Recent findings suggest that you can also run the model directly with ONNX Runtime, making it highly portable and cross-platform compatible. The example below demonstrates usage in Python, but the same approach can be applied in other languages (Java, C#, C++, etc.) as well.

Recent findings suggest that as with all models compatible with the Sentence Transformers library, EmbeddingGemma can be easily fine-tuned on your specific dataset. To showcase this, we'll be finetuning google/embeddinggemma-300m on the Medical Instruction and RetrIeval Dataset (MIRIAD) dataset, such that our finetuned model becomes particularly adept at finding passages up to 1000 tokens from scientific medical papers given detailed medical questions. These passages can be used as crucial context for a generative model to answer questions more effectively.

Below, you can explore each key component of the finetuning process using expandable tabs. Each tab contains the relevant code and a detailed explanation.

This code loads the EmbeddingGemma model from Hugging Face, with optional model card metadata for documentation and sharing. The SentenceTransformer class loads the model weights and configuration, while the model_card_data argument attaches metadata useful for inclusion in the automatically generated model card.

Recent findings suggest that this code loads the MIRIAD dataset, or rather, a copy that has been divided into train, eval, and test splits. Using a large, high-quality dataset ensures the model learns meaningful representations, while subsetting allows for faster experimentation. The load_dataset function fetches the dataset from Hugging Face Datasets, and the .select() method limits the number of samples for each split.

Recent findings suggest that this code defines the loss function for training, using Cached Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss (CMNRL). CMNRL is effective for retrieval tasks, as it uses in-batch negatives to efficiently train the model to distinguish between correct and incorrect pairs. The loss takes question-answer pairs and treats other answers in the batch as negatives, maximizing the distance between unrelated pairs in the embedding space. The mini_batch_size parameter controls the memory usage, but does not affect the training dynamics.

It's recommended to use this loss with a large per_device_train_batch_size in SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments and a low mini_batch_size in CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss for a strong training signal with low memory usage. Additionally, the NO_DUPLICATES batch sampler is recommended to avoid accidental false negatives.

Industry observers note that this code sets up all hyperparameters and configuration for training, evaluation, and logging. Proper training arguments are crucial for efficient, stable, and reproducible training. The arguments control batch sizes, learning rate, mixed precision, evaluation and saving frequency, and more. Notably, the prompts dictionary maps dataset columns to prompts used by the model to distinguish queries from documents.

It has been revealed that this code sets up an evaluator for information retrieval, using queries and a corpus to measure model performance. Evaluation during training helps monitor progress and avoid overfitting. The evaluator computes retrieval metrics (NDCG, MRR, Recall, Precision, MAP, etc.) by checking if the model retrieves the correct passages for each query. It can be run before, during, and after training, and the results will be logged and incorporated in the automatically generated model card.

Note that this snippet in particular uses all (1k) evaluation questions against a corpus of all (1k) evaluation passages and 30k training passages, for a total of 31k documents. Evaluating only against evaluation passages is too simple for the model.

This code initializes and runs the training loop, coordinating all components.

In a recent development, our fine-tuning process achieved a significant improvement of +0.0522 NDCG@10 on the test set, resulting in a model that comfortably outperforms any existing general-purpose embedding model on our specific task, at this model size. Additional time and compute investment would allow for even stronger results, such as hard negatives mining or training with more than 100k data pairs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that iâve been working on a ledger implementation in pure PostgreSQL called pgledger. As Iâve written about previously, I think more applications should use double-entry ledgers.

Sources indicate that however, once a ledger is integrated, it can be a bit hard to wrap your head around it visually. What are the money flows? What are the main set of accounts per user? Why is the balance in this account not what I expect?

In my work with companies, Iâve often tried to make the ledger more visual and understandable, either with a database dashboard like Metabase or with custom in-app code.

The same way that pgledger is meant to be a common, reusable ledger across applications, I thought we could have a common, reusable visualization tool. And thus pgledger-ui was born.

This is what it looks like to view a ledger account, showing the account details, the most common counterparty accounts, a chart of balance over time, and the detailed transfer entries:.

In general, pgledger-ui is pretty simple. It runs database queries and shows them in a webpage. There are some charts and extra aggregate information. And the whole thing is bundled into a single Go binary:.

Beyond this, there are a few main ideas baked into pgledger-ui:.

It has been revealed that often, when debugging an matter, you start by realizing a ledger account doesnât have the balance you expect. Then, you want to see the transfers in and out of that account. And maybe you want to trace a given metadata key across transfers (e.g. the payment_id). As you continue debugging, you may follow an account to a transfer to another account and so on. With pgledger-ui, each entity highlights the related entities, and you can click on any of them to trace a flow. This even includes metadata keys, so you can see related transfers which share the same key/value pair.

Recent findings suggest that it should be easy to find what you want, so pgledger-ui has a single, universal search box. You can search by id, account name, idempotency key, metadata values, etc., and it will show you all matches across all entities. For example, if you name your accounts hierarchically (e.g. user01.available, user01.pending, etc.) you can search for user01 and see all accounts and transfers for that user.

Sources indicate that I like interfaces which are information dense, without being overwhelming. The goal is to show a lot of useful information in each page, and make it easy to scan for what you need.

It has been revealed that normally, when you query data from a database, you get row-based results. However, I find that visualizing ledgers in a columnar format is often more useful.

Sources indicate that for example, say you are looking at all of the transfer entries for a given payment. The results may come back like this:.

But a columnar view of that same data looks like:.

(Example from the pgledger reconciliation.sql.out script).

In a recent development, postgreSQL calls this a crosstab (or crosstabview in psql). A pivot table in a spreadsheet may be similar. And itâs a common way to visualize a ledger1.

This type of view exists in pgledger-ui as well, especially if youâre tracing a flow via a metadata key:.

And you can separate the in/out flows, making it resemble a standard ledger T-account view:.

Industry observers note that please check out pgledger-ui, and Iâd love to hear what you think, especially if you work with pgledger or other ledgers today. Are there other useful visualizations or tools youâve seen in this space? And if pgledger-ui is something that you are interested in using, please let me know.

TrendForce sees supply outpacing demand in 2027, though cheaper flash won't fix the DRAM squeeze.

NAND flash prices could start falling next year as Chinese cloud operators cut enterprise SSD orders, helping push the market toward oversupply.

Taiwan-based market intelligence firm TrendForce claims Chinese cloud service providers are grappling with GPU shortages, high inventories, and fierce competition over AI token pricing.

As a result, they have reduced their total enterprise SSD orders for 2027 by a substantial amount. Although TrendForce doesn't specify any figures, it claims the cutbacks in China are large enough to outweigh the additional demand coming from US-based cloud operators.

But don't get too excited: TrendForce forecasts overall NAND flash contract prices falling by 0-5 percent quarter on quarter in early 2027, with all product categories entering a downturn from the second quarter.

Falling orders are only half the story. Manufacturers are also increasing output, while weaker consumer electronics sales could further depress demand.

Industry observers note that strong demand for high-performance storage in the US continues to drive manufacturers to expand capacity and upgrade to newer process technologies. At the same time, the rising adoption of quad-level cell (QLC) technology and increasing number of layers in the NAND chips will further boost bit output, TrendForce observes.

Some suppliers may go slower on their expansion looks in response to sluggish consumer demand, but the firm still expects global NAND flash output, measured in storage capacity, to grow by 25 to 30 percent in 2027.

US restrictions on access to advanced AI chips could put Chinese cloud operators under further pressure. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has introduced fresh restrictions on sales of GPUs, and on remote access to them via the cloud.

The newly introduced restrictions "set everyone back in China," as The Register reported.

TrendForce adds the caveat to its forecast that its market outlook depends on factors such as the pace of inventory reduction among Chinese CSPs, further changes to the restrictions on overseas GPU procurement, and whether device makers continue reducing storage capacities in 2028.

It has been revealed that sadly, cheaper NAND wouldn't resolve the separate squeeze on DRAM supplies. The situation, caused by memory makers opting to produce high-margin products for the AI market rather than mainstream chips, has already increased prices of PCs in Europe by double-digit percentages, leading to a fall in shipments as buyers balk at the cost. ®.

Tech Report: mmBERT: ModernBERT goes Multilingual

📅 09 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this blog post introduces mmBERT, a state-of-the-art massively multilingual encoder model trained on 3T+ tokens of text in over 1800 languages.
  • If you are interested in trying out the models yourself, some example boilerplate is available at the end of this blogpost!
  • Sources indicate that mmBERT was trained on a carefully curated multilingual dataset totaling over 3T tokens across three distinct training phases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this blog post introduces mmBERT, a state-of-the-art massively multilingual encoder model trained on 3T+ tokens of text in over 1800 languages. It indicates significant performance and speed improvements over previous multilingual models, being the first to improve upon XLM-R, while also developing fresh strategies for effectively learning low-resource languages. mmBERT builds upon ModernBERT for a blazingly fast architecture, and adds novel components to enable efficient multilingual learning.

If you are interested in trying out the models yourself, some example boilerplate is available at the end of this blogpost!

Sources indicate that mmBERT was trained on a carefully curated multilingual dataset totaling over 3T tokens across three distinct training phases. The foundation of our training data consists of three primary open-source and high-quality web crawls that enable both multilingual coverage and data quality:.

Sources indicate that DCLM and Filtered DCLM provides the highest quality English content available, serving as the backbone for strong English performance (with the filtered data coming from Dolmino). This dataset represents state-of-the-art web filtering techniques and forms a crucial component. Due to the high quality of this data, we use a signficantly higher proportion of English than previous generation multilingual encoder models (up to 18%).

FineWeb2 delivers broad multilingual web content covering over 1,800 languages. This dataset enables our extensive multilingual coverage while maintaining reasonable quality standards across diverse language families and scripts.

According to recent reports, fineWeb2-HQ consists of a filtered subset of FineWeb2 focusing on 20 high-resource languages. This filtered version provides higher-quality multilingual content that bridges the gap between English-only filtered data and broad multilingual coverage.

The training data also incorporates specialized corpora from Dolma, MegaWika v2, ProLong and more: code repositories (StarCoder, ProLong), academic content (ArXiv, PeS2o), reference materials (Wikipedia, textbooks), and community discussions (StackExchange), along with instruction and mathematical datasets.

In a recent development, the key innovation in our data approach is the progressive language inclusion strategy shown in Figure 1. At each phase we progressively sample from a flatter distribution (i.e. closer to uniform), while also adding new languages. This means that high resource languages like Russian start off with a high percentage of the data (i.e. 9%) and then in the last phase of training end around half of that. We start with 60 high-resource languages during pre-training, expand to 110 languages during mid-training, and finally include all 1,833 languages from FineWeb2 during the decay phase. This allows us to maximize the impact of limited low-resource language data without excess reptitions and while maintaining high overall data quality.

mmBERT builds upon the ModernBERT architecture but introduces several key innovations for multilingual learning:.

It has been revealed that we use the same core architecture as ModernBERT-base with 22 layers and 1152 intermediate dimensions, but switch to the Gemma 2 tokenizer to better handle multilingual text. The base model has 110M non-embedding parameters (307M total due to the larger vocabulary), while the small variant has 42M non-embedding parameters (140M total).

Our training follows a carefully designed three-phase schedule:.

Inverse Mask Ratio Schedule: Instead of using a fixed masking rate, we progressively reduce the mask ratio from 30% → 15% → 5% across training phases. This allows the model to learn basic representations with higher masking early on, then focus on more nuanced understanding with lower masking rates.

Annealed Language Learning: We dynamically adjust the temperature for multilingual data sampling from τ=0.7 → 0.5 → 0.3. This creates a progression from high-resource language bias toward more uniform sampling, enabling the model to build a strong multilingual foundation before learning low-resource languages.

According to recent reports, progressive Language Addition: Rather than training on all languages simultaneously, we strategically add languages at each phase (60 → 110 → 1,833). This maximizes learning efficiency by avoiding excessive epochs on limited low-resource data while still achieving strong performance.

Model Merging: We train three different variants during the decay phase (English-focused, 110-language, and all-language) and use TIES merging to combine their strengths into the final model.

English Performance: On the English GLUE benchmark (Table 1), mmBERT base achieves strong performance, substantially outperforming other multilingual models like XLM-R (multilingual RoBERTa) base and mGTE base, while remaining competitive to English-only models despite less than 25% of the mmBERT training data being English.

In a recent development, multilingual Performance: mmBERT indicates significant improvements on XTREME benchmark compared to XLM-R as demonstrated in Table 2. Notable gains include strong performance on XNLI classification, substantial improvements in question answering tasks like TyDiQA, and competitive results across PAWS-X and XCOPA for cross-lingual understanding.

The model performs well across most categories, with the exception of some structured prediction tasks like NER and POS tagging, likely due to tokenizer differences that affect word boundary detection. On these categories, it performs about the same as the previous generation, but can be applied to more languages.

English Retrieval: Even though mmBERT is designed for massively multilingual settings, in the MTEB v2 English benchmarks (Table 3), mmBERT shows significant gains over previous multilingual models and even ties the capabilities of English-only models like ModernBERT!

Multilingual Retrieval: mmBERT shows consistent improvements on MTEB v2 multilingual benchmarks compared to other models (Table 4).

It has been revealed that code Retrieval: Due to the modern tokenizer (based on Gemma 2) mmBERT also indicates strong coding performance (Table 5), making mmBERT suitable for any type of textual data. The only model that outperforms it is EuroBERT, which was able to use the non-publicly accessible Stack v2 dataset.

It has been revealed that one of mmBERT's most significant novel features is demonstrating that low-resource languages can be effectively learned during the short decay phase of training. We validated this approach by testing on languages only introduced during the final 100B token decay phase.

Dramatic Performance Gains: Testing on TiQuaD (Tigrinya) and FoQA (Faroese), we observed substantial improvements when these languages were included in the decay phase, as shown in Figure 2. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our progressive language learning approach.

Competitive with Large Models: Despite only seeing these languages in the final training phase, mmBERT achieves performance levels that exceed much larger models. On Faroese question answering where LLMs have been benchmarked, mmBERT outperforms Google Gemini 2.5 Pro and OpenAI o3.

In a recent development, rapid Learning Mechanism: The success of decay-phase language learning stems from the model's ability to leverage its strong multilingual foundation built during earlier phases. When exposed to new languages, the model can quickly adapt existing cross-lingual representations rather than learning from scratch.

Model Merging Benefits: The final mmBERT models successfully retain most of the decay-phase improvements while benefiting from the English-focused and high-resource variants through TIES merging.

mmBERT delivers substantial efficiency gains over previous multilingual encoder models through architectural improvements inherited from ModernBERT:.

Throughput Performance: mmBERT processes text significantly faster than existing multilingual models across various sequence lengths, as demonstrated in Figure 3. Both the small and base models show substantial speed improvements over previous multilingual encoders.

Modern Architecture Benefits: The efficiency gains come from two main technical improvements:.

Sequence Length Scaling: Unlike older models limited to 512 tokens, mmBERT handles up to 8,192 tokens efficiently while maintaining high throughput. This makes it suitable for longer document processing tasks that are increasingly common in multilingual applications.

Energy Efficiency: The combination of better throughput and modern architecture results in lower computational costs for inference, making mmBERT more practical for production deployments where multilingual support is needed at scale.

These efficiency improvements make mmBERT not just more accurate than previous multilingual encoders, but also significantly more practical for real usage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Company still has to contend with massive compute obligations and the threat of open models, neither of which Dario Amodei is worried about, he claims.

Welcome to the world of public AI frontier labs: Anthropic is now a publicly-held organization with its Thursday IPO, and investors are clamoring for a piece of the pie, for now anyway.

Recent findings suggest that that $83 IPO price didn’t last long, with shares rocketing to $111.50 by the time the public could get their hands on them at the end of the initial auction. That means that the company was valued at around $2 trillion as of the public availability of the 980 million shares it put up for sale, a 34 percent increase over the IPO price.

At just under six years old, Anthropic’s meteoric rise to that valuation has sent investors into a frenzy despite uncertainties surrounding the company’s future profitability. As we’ve noted, Anthropic is on the hook for nearly $1 trillion in compute obligations that could drag its profitability prospects down if any one of a number of scenarios happens to materialize.

Amodei was on hand to address some of those questions with CNBC this morning following the opening of markets on his company’s big day.

When asked about the risk Anthropic’s massive compute bills to its bottom line, Amodei admitted the manufacturer’s needs are difficult to predict, and that - get this - they try to err on the low side.

That’s right: The $900 billion in infrastructure and compute commitments that Anthropic revealed in a recent regulatory filing, which could end up surpassing $1T in short order, might just be an underestimate of what the manufacturer will need in coming months and years.

Not to worry, though, the Anthropic CEO insisted: It’s worth it.

“We’re willing to put into place these very large compute spends because, historically, we’ve seen that it pays off,” Amodei told CNBC’s Ross Sorkin, adding that the returns on the cognitive capabilities of its fresh models are “so high” as to make all that spending worth it - eventually, one would assume based on his comments, Anthropic is sure to come out on top.

But what of the threat of open models that could undermine the constant push at Anthropic and other frontier labs to create the most power-hungry, resource-intensive, and powerful AI? Bah, that’s not a problem either.

Frontier model makers like Anthropic, Amodei said, have already proven that they can do the heavy lifting at the bleeding edge, so you can trust it to make reliable models that are cheaper and less capable, too.

“Anthropic can compete both at and away from the frontier,” The Anthropic CEO mentioned.

Whether that’ll mean long-term success for investors is another thing altogether. Mozilla president Mark Surman doesn’t think valuation translates into long-term success, for one. He told The Register this morning that the one thing he consistently hears from developers is that they want AI they can control, not rent from a frontier lab. As Amodei suggested in his comments, Anthropic is aware that those with less intense AI needs might not choose its models, and that could harm the manufacturer.

According to recent reports, “Pushing AI toward open source matters so much right now,” Surman remarked in an email. “Mozilla’s own research this year found that open source models account for a third of all tokens, while the gap with the best closed models is down to about 3.3 per cent.”.

In other words, keep an eye on that Anthropic stock - it might be hot now, but reality could still catch up to the manufacturer with the biggest-ever IPO.

In a recent development, “The market is already moving,” Surman said. “No valuation changes that.” ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pick up your work exactly where life made you stop — on the same machine or from elsewhere.

Mercurius gives you long‑lived graphical sessions that you can leave, return to, and resume whether you’re on the same laptop or somewhere else on the network. The session model works locally without any networking at all; the network simply lets your sessions inhabit more powerful machines when you want them to.

Industry observers note that sometimes life interrupts. Work calls, dinner is ready, or you need to switch tasks. Mercurius treats sessions as first-class objects so your applications belong to the session, not the physical device in front of you.

In a recent development, suspend a coding session, switch to a gaming session, and resume either one later with every window exactly as you left it. Built for powerful workstations, modern GPUs, and fast local networks, Mercurius uses the network to extend your experience, not to justify its existence.

Sources indicate that it used to be normal to share the big, expensive computer in the corner. Today everyone has a laptop, but the economics of computing have changed again: RAM and GPUs are costly, and workstation‑class machines deliver far more capability than most people carry around. Mercurius lets you use that capability without giving up the convenience of your own environment.

In a recent development, mercurius keeps your work on your own machines, so you’re never at the mercy of a cloud subscription just to read your own documents. With the rising cost of local RAM and high‑end GPUs, sharing the expensive computer again is a smart alternative. Mercurius lets an organisation concentrate its investment in a few powerful GPU‑rich workstations and make full use of them, instead of buying every developer a high‑end laptop that can’t run the heavy workloads anyway.

  • Recent findings suggest that agents can read data, call APIs, change records and trigger other agents using service accounts, OAuth grants, API tokens, workload identities or delegated sessions.
  • Sources indicate that the platform establishes behavioral baselines around the systems agents access, the actions they perform and the identities they use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mitiga debuted AI Agent Security on November 19, 2026, and made the agentless platform immediately available. It is designed to discover and monitor AI agents across cloud, software-as-a-service (SaaS) and identity systems, then contain suspicious activity through customers’ existing security integrations.

Recent findings suggest that agents can read data, call APIs, change records and trigger other agents using service accounts, OAuth grants, API tokens, workload identities or delegated sessions. Co-founder and chief technology officer Ofer Maor described the resulting visibility problem: “An agent doesn’t need to break in when it already holds the credential. To the audit log, it looks like a valid login.”.

Sources indicate that the platform establishes behavioral baselines around the systems agents access, the actions they perform and the identities they use. It compares live activity with permissions and static configuration to surface privilege drift and unauthorized access, then correlates cloud, SaaS, identity and AI activity into a unified incident record. Activity Flow maps consumers and non-human identities through AI platforms and connectors to the applications they reached.

It has been revealed that no gateway, SDK, proxy or code change inside an agent is required. Mitiga instead works from logs and APIs that supported platforms already produce, allowing deployment outside the agent’s execution path. Retained logs can also support investigations into agent activity that occurred before the platform was deployed.

Coverage spans homegrown agents built on services such as Bedrock and Azure AI Foundry, sanctioned vendor agents connected through OAuth grants, and employee-connected coding assistants, personal AI tools and unreviewed MCP servers or skills. Mitiga’s four named scenarios are third-party agent compromise, homegrown-agent overreach, coding-agent and MCP supply-chain threats, and cascading actions in which one compromised agent triggers tools, services or other agents.

For coding-agent supply-chain risks, the free Skillgate scanner checks skills and MCP servers for hidden instructions or credential-exfiltration paths before an agent acts. If the agent has already run, Mitiga reconstructs what the developer’s credentials did next.

Mitiga reports three operating figures: 95% of security-operations-center workflows automated, 100% of alerts triaged with an auditable verdict, and under three minutes from event collection through triage to an actionable response. The underlying Cloud Security Data Lake normalizes telemetry from more than 50 platforms and retains it for more than 1,000 days.

The product documentation explicitly distinguishes Mitiga from an inline guardrail: it does not block an action before that action occurs. Detection latency depends on the telemetry source, and coverage is limited to agents whose actions appear in supported cloud, SaaS, identity or AI sources.

Prompt-level signals are available only where supported platform logs expose them, including Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Agentforce and Copilot logs. Without that visibility, Mitiga detects the resulting downstream behavior.

Supported responses include revoking a token or session, quarantining an identity and reversing a change through customer integrations. Reversal depends on what each integration supports. For enterprises deploying the platform, log coverage and integration support therefore form part of its effective security boundary, determining where Mitiga can investigate an agent’s activity and which containment actions are available.

Breaking: Jupyter Agents: training LLMs to reason with notebooks

📅 10 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The past year has been all about giving LLMs more tools and autonomy to solve more complex and open ended tasks.
  • A natural way to display multi-step code execution together with reasoning is within a Jupyter Notebook, which consists of code and markdown cells.
  • While large models are starting to show useful behavior, the key question is how we can continue improving them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The past year has been all about giving LLMs more tools and autonomy to solve more complex and open ended tasks. The goal of the Jupyter Agent is to give the model the ultimate tool: code execution.

A natural way to display multi-step code execution together with reasoning is within a Jupyter Notebook, which consists of code and markdown cells. So we built Jupyter Agent to act as an agent that can execute code directly inside a Jupyter notebook and use this environment to solve data analysis and data science tasks. Think of it like Cursor, but living natively inside your data science workflow.We built a demo of this vision with Qwen-3 Coder, currently one of the strongest coding models. This is a follow-up to our earlier work on jupyter-agent (v1).

While large models are starting to show useful behavior, the key question is how we can continue improving them. To this end, we focus on strengthening smaller models to perform well on agentic data science tasks as they presently struggle to compete with the large models.

The goal of this project is to build a pipeline to first generate high-quality training data, then fine-tune an existing small model, and finally evaluate whether the model's performance improves on relevant benchmarks.

Let’s begin with the last step: selecting a strong benchmark for evaluating models on data science tasks.

In order to understand if we are making progress towards better data science agents we need a benchmark to measure such capabilities. Last year, in partnership with Adyen, we introduced the DABStep benchmark: a way to evaluate data science agents on realistic tasks. The setup is simple: provide the LLM with datasets and ask it to answer non-trivial data questions.

Sources indicate that this benchmark remains challenging for today’s LLMs — e.g. the best out-of-the-box model is Claude 4 Sonnet which reaches not even 20% accuracy on the hard tasks.You can explore the live leaderboard here.

In a recent development, now that we identified a good benchmark we can try to climb it! We set out to build a dataset for fine-tuning such that even a small data agent model could perform well on DABStep.

Our first choice was Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507: extremely small (fast to iterate with, easy to run), yet strong enough to act in agentic scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that not great — but a promising starting point, since it left a lot of room for improvement. Let's see how we can improve it!

A core aspect of agents that sets it apart from a pure chat model is the scaffolding built around the model to steer its behaviour. The evaluation script in DABStep for example uses smolagents to execute code. Smolagents comes with predefined behaviors, prompting structures, and expected formats.

In a recent development, we also studied the Qwen-Agent codebase, where the authors tailoring scaffolding to the model. This makes sense: Claude Code, for example, works shockingly well with Claude Sonnet because their scaffolding is aligned.

So, we restructured our scaffolding:.

Results: accuracy jumped from 44.4% → 59.7% (easy split). 🚀.

With simplified scaffolding in place, we focused on fine-tuning Qwen3-4B for data science agentic tasks.

The recipe to improve a model on a certain task or behaviour is to train it on data that reflects the tasks as closely as possible. A natural starting point is to look at real Jupyter Notebooks and find notebooks that align closely with the task that we strategy to tackle, namely data analysis.

Kaggle notebooks offer a wealth of high quality data analysis notebooks and are made available by Kaggle:.

Now that we have good results with a base model it's time to build a dataset that will help us improve it even further. We designed a multi-stage pipeline using Datatrove to clean and prepare Kaggle notebooks at scale.

We started with ~2TB of Kaggle notebooks and reduced it to ~250GB reusing our work from the BigCode project. As part of the StarCoder2 training data processing the notebooks (without output cells) were already deduplicated. Most Kaggle notebooks are small variations or near-identical copies, so this step was essential.Key insight: ~90% of raw notebooks are duplicates, which would have skewed training if left unfiltered.

Industry observers note that most Kaggle notebooks reference external datasets via Kaggle metadata. To make sure the code inside notebooks could actually run, we built a pipeline that automatically fetched these linked datasets. This step was crucial, since many notebooks would otherwise be incomplete or non-executable.

According to recent reports, using the kagglehub package, we downloaded thousands of datasets — about 5TB in total. To keep things manageable and relevant:.

By the end, we had a rich collection of executable notebooks paired with their datasets, providing the foundation for training agents in realistic, runnable environments.

We scored notebooks based on educational quality using Qwen3-32B. We saw that using the whole notebook was not optimal, as many contained trivial or broken code. Our educational scoring approach is detailed in edu_scoring.py.

In a recent development, TL;DR: We assigned each notebook a score from 1–5 based on clarity, completeness, and educational value, and kept only those above a chosen threshold. This filtering removed about 70% of the notebooks.

Sources indicate that this is similar to the insight from the BeyondWeb paper, which indicated that using high-quality data is better for synthetic data generation — a step we relied on for QA (Question-Answer) generation. This helped the model learn from “high quality” notebooks instead of noisy ones.

Recent findings suggest that we excluded notebooks about training LLMs or unrelated to data analysis. We also removed notebooks that didn’t actually use datasets through an automated LLM-based filtering process using Qwen3-32B. The implementation of filtering can be found in extract_packages_and_files.py.

TL;DR: We prompted Qwen3-32B to identify and remove notebooks that either (1) had nothing to do with data analysis, or (2) didn’t actually use datasets. This step removed about 20% of the notebooks.

This ensured we trained only on relevant data science tasks.

Using the cleaned notebooks, we generated question–answer pairs using Qwen3-32B. The questions and answer are grounded in the real notebook traces so the QA pairs are based on real code execution results. Prompt design: we asked the LLM to produce natural questions that could realistically be asked of the dataset, then validated whether the notebook provided a correct answer.

Challenge: We had to try many prompts to get higher-difficulty questions because LLMs tended to generate trivial ones like "what is the size of the dataset".Insight: We broke this into two steps because LLMs tended to hallucinate answers:.

The complete prompting strategy and implementation is available in generate_qa.py.

Finally we want to generate clean code execution traces since even the original notebooks after processing are often open ended and verbose with lots of irrelevant parts. However, we want our Jupyter Agent to get to the result efficiently. To generate cleaner notebook traces for training we generated traces synthetically based on the original notebooks.We have prompted Qwen-3-Coder-480B model to generate a jupyter notebook code to answer the question from the previously generated synthetic QA pair. Traces captured step-by-step code execution, including intermediate outputs, which are crucial for agent training.

We used E2B for our agent to solve the synthetic QA pairs, which required fetching Kaggle datasets so the code could actually run via E2B.

Challenge 1: Many datasets were unavailable.Trick: Since LLMs are strong at code and have a decent world model, we prompted them to act as a code interpreter when the dataset was missing.

Challenge 2: Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B model does not support thinking mode - how can we extract code commentary? By default it often outputs just a brief comment followed by several steps of code execution. However, we'd like some reasoning or comments between every cell. Trick: When switching from Qwen3-32B to Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B we noticed that often output message content was empty. This turns out to be a previously known quirk of Qwen3-Coder models in which when using tool calling the model would not return an empty assistant response. We enforce some text commentary through tooling by passing 'comment' as a required field in the code execution tool call. This way when non-reasoning model is used for code cell generation it will by default output some description of its actions from 1st POV, emulating the thinking traces structure.

In a recent development, note: the generated final answer in the notebook may vary from the answer specified in the QA pair. This is caused by the fact that the agent model could use data preprocessing methods and steps different from the original Kaggle notebook and the synthetic question would not usually specify them. This discrepancy is normal and lays the foundation for a fresh exciting research direction of how language models tend to treat data analysis and whether they do it differently from humans. For full transparency we keep both LLM-generated final answer and original answer from the real Kaggle notebook as a signal of model's performance. We encourage the community to try different dataset mixes to see how they can push performance even further.

We truncated overly long outputs and filtered out trivial traces to prevent content length problems and keep only high-quality traces.We kept non-trivial, multi-turn traces aligned with DABStep-style tasks.The resulting Jupyter Agent Dataset became the foundation for SFT on Qwen3-4B models with 51k synthetic notebooks and almost 0.2B tokens.

With this dataset in hand, the natural next step is to see whether it actually helps our model become a stronger data science agent. Let’s move on to the training pipeline and evaluate the impact!

With the curated dataset ready, we turned to the key question: does this data actually help the model get better at solving data analysis tasks? To find out, we set up a simple fine-tuning pipeline and ran experiments to measure the impact of training on our synthetic notebooks.

Some training steps turned out to be particularly interesting and gave us useful insights:.

Our complete training implementation, including hyperparameter configurations and template adaptations, is available in our finetuning directory in our repo.

Industry observers note that first, we generated our final dataset using Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B which contains high quality code and short reasoning-like traces. Afterwards, we started our training and we have experimented with various configurations like PEFT/adapters vs. full-parameter tuning, learning rate, number of epochs, adding noise and others. We found out, that full-parameter fine-tuning allows the model to learn and replicate the Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B behavior response quality better with shorter supporting commentary fitting more to the data analysis task without unnecessary long reasoning.

It has been revealed that we have done a small ablation study on the impact of no. training epochs:.

We observe that it is beneficial to have a bit more epochs than usual for SFT with lower learning rate and higher neftune noise (7). Finally, we compare our trained models with implemented scaffolding to define the pure impact of our training dataset. In summary, we can see up to 36%/22% boost on DABStep easy score compared with base/scaffolded model:.

We can also see, that the hard score can increase too even though our dataset is focused on easier questions:.

From figures above one can notice a noticeable impact of both fresh scaffolding and tuning on our synthetic notebooks. This makes Qwen-4B (with our pipeline + scaffolding) a state-of-the-art small-model agent on DABStep.

In practice, the model can now solve a wide range of realistic Kaggle-style data analysis tasks with consistent execution.It’s not yet strong enough for the hardest queries, but we’ve shown that even small models can become powerful agents when paired with the right data and scaffolding.

Sources indicate that these results demonstrate that even small models can become powerful data science agents with the right training approach. Ready to try it yourself? We've made everything openly available so you can experiment with our fine-tuned models and dataset.

We openly release best-performing checkpoints of tuned Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 together with the training dataset, which you can try out and experiment with:.

You can load Jupyter Agent Dataset in just a couple of lines using the following code:.

You can also use sourced Kaggle datasets directly with E2B code execution using the following code:.

You use tuned Jupyter Agent Qwen-based models following the Qwen documentation code:.

For Thinking model you can decode both thinking response and content using the next code:.

Maybe this will lead to… Jupyter-Agent 3. 😉.

We hope that our findings will inspire others to continue progress in developing more powerful notebook coding agents and we're excited to see what the community builds next. Dive into our jupyter-agent dataset on the 🤗 Hub and explore the codebase at https://github.com/huggingface/jupyter-agent to start your own experiments on agents for jupyter notebooks.

Industry News: XXRI-OS explores the lowest end of the Linux desktop

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Less is more, but this distro explores exactly how much less.
  • Newly introduced Linux distros seem to appear daily, but far too few distinguish themselves by being smaller and simpler.
  • In a recent development, XXRI OS is a fairly upcoming desktop Linux distro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less is more, but this distro explores exactly how much less.

Newly introduced Linux distros seem to appear daily, but far too few distinguish themselves by being smaller and simpler.

In a recent development, XXRI OS is a fairly upcoming desktop Linux distro. It has a snazzy-looking website, complete with an amusing URL, and along similar lines, its GitHub page has a very heavily formatted README. Nonetheless, this is not another over-complex opinionated slopfest of an OS with built-in AI, bizarre keystrokes, and several proprietary components. It's almost the reverse.

The main download is just 287.4 MB, and that's the full distro, not a minimalist installer that fetches most of the OS over your internet connection. We installed it in a VirtualBox VM. It took 675 MB of disk space, and in the graphical desktop, when we opened a terminal window, it reported just 75 MB of RAM in use with the desktop and terminal running. We are restraining ourselves hard when we say that those are unusually low numbers for the 2020s. We would expect most cut-down lightweight Linux distros to use around five to 10 times as much disk space or memory.

It has been revealed that the current release of XXRI-OS is version 2.7. XXRI OS 1.0 came out in May 2025, making this a young project with five published releases already behind it. It also has much deeper roots: it is based on the existing and much older Tiny Core Linux. The Reg FOSS desk last looked at Tiny Core Linux 15 back in March 2024 and the project is still going strong: the latest version is version 17.1.

Tiny Core Linux is a marvel, but there are prices to pay for somehow getting a graphical Linux desktop into a 23 MB download. It runs from RAM and uses its own extension-based package system, which can make adding components and managing updates unfamiliar territory. XXRI OS takes TCL and turns it into a slightly more conventional desktop.

Recent findings suggest that it installs to disk in the usual way, and it includes the core functions that most people would expect from their OS in 2026. It has a file manager, a text editor, a media player, a simple app store for adding further components, and a settings app including an update manager. It even includes its own web browser, and there are both x86-32 and x86-64 variants.

It has been revealed that the desktop layout has a floating dock at bottom center, and the icons are unlabelled. To save you some guesswork, though, floating just to the left of the dock is an icon with a grid of dots, which is an app launcher. The icons in that do have text labels underneath, so you can learn which symbol denotes which function from here.

We plan to experiment more with this remarkable little OS and see how well it runs on the oldest, slowest boxes in the Irish Sea wing of Vulture Towers, but we like what we see so far. It's an impressive experiment in how low Linux can go and remain useful. While Tiny Core Linux goes down to Windows 95 levels of resource usage, XXRI OS has a more usable Windows 2000-level baseline. Over a quarter of a century later, that is nearly unbeatable. ®.

AWS Enables Default Monitoring for SageMaker AI Inference Endpoints

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Web Services (AWS) enabled default monitoring for eligible Amazon SageMaker AI generative AI inference endpoints on November 19, 2026, adding AWS Health findings for latency drift, idle GPU capacity and missed serving optimizations.
  • Sources indicate that the monitoring requires no setup on endpoints that use vLLM serving containers and GPU instances.
  • In a recent development, the announcement extends the optimized generative AI inference recommendations that AWS introduced on April 22, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Web Services (AWS) enabled default monitoring for eligible Amazon SageMaker AI generative AI inference endpoints on November 19, 2026, adding AWS Health findings for latency drift, idle GPU capacity and missed serving optimizations.

Sources indicate that the monitoring requires no setup on endpoints that use vLLM serving containers and GPU instances. It reads endpoint-level latency, GPU utilization and serving configuration, not request or response content. The target is gradual drift after deployment as traffic, prompt lengths, serving software and model resource requirements change.

In a recent development, the announcement extends the optimized generative AI inference recommendations that AWS introduced on April 22, 2026. That workflow lets users choose cost, latency or throughput as the objective, compare up to three instance types, and benchmark configurations on real GPUs with NVIDIA AIPerf. It also supports benchmarks of existing production endpoints; the new layer adds ongoing observation and notifications to that user-initiated decision process.

Latency-drift findings compare median (p50) end-to-end latency and median time to first token with the endpoint’s own preceding week. Because the baseline is historical, owners do not need to set a threshold in advance. A resulting benchmark tests tensor parallelism settings and alternative instance types or sizes.

Sources indicate that other findings cover GPUs that remain well below capacity, supported but disabled speculative decoding, untuned GPU kernels, and serving containers missing newer performance improvements or patches for critical and high-severity vulnerabilities. For unused capacity, the benchmark tests cheaper instance types and smaller sizes at observed peak traffic. Configuration tests compare the current setup with speculative decoding enabled, tuned kernels or an updated container, as applicable.

AWS’s examples are walkthrough illustrations, not fleet-wide measurements: one reports median time to first token rising about 200 milliseconds week over week, while another reports even the busiest GPU using 12% or less of capacity for most of a week.

Findings arrive through AWS Health and email. Each endpoint gets at most one notification at a time covering all applicable findings, AWS limits how many an account receives at once, and notifications are specific to the endpoint’s AWS Region.

A notification states what was observed, why it matters for latency, capacity or cost, and a recommended action, with estimates labeled as estimates. It is an observation rather than a completed benchmark. The action opens an agentic experience in SageMaker Studio with the endpoint and its observed traffic prefilled.

It has been revealed that after the user confirms, the agent generates an editable SageMaker Python SDK notebook using the endpoint’s model and a traffic profile derived from its metrics. The notebook tags the recommendation job with the AWS Health event so results can be traced to the finding. The job compares the current configuration with alternatives on response time, throughput and cost per million tokens, using separate compute; production does not change until the user applies a result.

Recent findings suggest that AWS recommends applying a selected configuration to one production variant first while keeping the existing configuration available for rollback. Holding or dismissing a finding is also a normal outcome, and the notification remains in AWS Health event history.

Monitoring carries no additional GPU cost. Benchmarks use standard SageMaker AI charges or an existing machine-learning reservation, and acting on a finding requires a SageMaker Studio domain, AWS Identity and Access Management permissions to run recommendation jobs and revision endpoints, and sufficient benchmark-instance quota.

Recent findings suggest that customers can manage delivery through AWS User Notifications and optionally schedule recurring recommendations, such as monthly runs. Setting the OPT_OUT_TRACKING environment variable on a model container stops collection of that endpoint’s engine metrics, GPU metrics and startup configuration details, and prevents its notifications.

Sources indicate that support for an optimization does not guarantee a benefit. AWS notes speculative-decoding results depend on concurrency and prompt and response lengths and can differ between peak and off-peak traffic. That distinction defines the feature’s practical role: default telemetry supplies the warning, while the benchmark determines whether a possible saving or speedup holds at the traffic that matters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the pace of AI development today is breathtaking. Every single day, hundreds of newly introduced models appear on the Hugging Face Hub, some are specialized variants of popular base models like Llama or Qwen, others feature novel architectures or have been trained from scratch for specific domains. Whether it's a medical AI trained on clinical data, a coding assistant optimized for a particular programming language, or a multilingual model fine-tuned for specific cultural contexts, the Hugging Face Hub has become the beating heart of open-source AI innovation.

But here's the challenge: finding an amazing model is just the beginning. What happens when you discover a model that's 90% perfect for your use case, but you need that extra 10% of customization? Traditional fine-tuning infrastructure is complex, expensive, and often requires significant DevOps expertise to set up and maintain.

This is exactly the gap that Together AI and Hugging Face are bridging today. We're announcing a powerful new capability that makes the entire Hugging Face Hub available for fine-tuning using Together AI's infrastructure. Now, any compatible LLM on the Hub, whether it's from Meta or an individual contributor, can be fine-tuned with the same ease and reliability you expect from Together's platform.🚀.

Here's all it takes to start fine-tuning a HF model on the Together AI platform:.

Industry observers note that that's it! Your model will be trained on Together's infrastructure and can be deployed for inference, downloaded or even uploaded back to the Hub! For private repositories, simply add your HF token with hf_api_token="hf_xxxxxxxxxxxx".

As seen in the example above, when you fine-tune a Hugging Face model on Together AI, you actually specify two models:.

In a recent development, think of the base model as a "training template." It tells our system how to optimally allocate GPU resources, configure memory usage, set up the training pipeline, and prepare the model for inference. Your custom model should have a similar architecture, approximate size, and sequence length to the base model for optimal results.

As seen in the example above, if you want to fine-tune HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct (which uses Llama architecture), you'd use togethercomputer/llama-2-7b-chat as your base model template, because they share the same underlying architecture.

Sources indicate that the integration works bidirectionally. Together AI can pull any compatible public model from the Hugging Face Hub for training, and with the proper API tokens, it can download models private repositories as well. After training, your fine-tuned model can be automatically pushed back onto the Hub if you've specified hf_output_repo_name, making it available for sharing with your team or the broader community.

In a recent development, in general, all CausalLM models under 100B params are intended to work. For a comprehensive walkthrough on how to choose base and custom models and much more, read our full guide!

This integration solves a real problem many of us have faced: finding a great model on Hugging Face but not having the infrastructure to actually fine-tune it for your specific needs. Now you can go from discovering a promising model to having a customized version running in production with just a few API calls.

Recent findings suggest that the big win here is removing friction. Instead of spending days setting up training infrastructure or being limited to whatever models are officially supported by various platforms, you can now experiment with any compatible model from the Hub. Found a specialized coding model that's close to what you need? Train it on your data!📈.

It has been revealed that for teams, this means faster iteration cycles. You can test multiple model approaches quickly, build on community innovations, and even use your own fine-tuned models as starting points for further customization.

Beta consumers and early adopters of this feature are already seeing results across diverse use cases.

Slingshot AI has integrated this capability directly into their model development pipeline. Rather than being limited to Together's model catalog, they can now run parts of the training pipeline on their own infrastructure, upload those models to the Hub, and then perform continued fine-tuning of those models using the Together AI fine-tuning platform. This has dramatically accelerated their development cycles and allowed them to easily experiment with a broad variety of model variants.

Recent findings suggest that parsed has demonstrated the power of this approach in their work showing how small, well-tuned open-source models can outperform much larger closed models. By fine-tuning models on carefully curated datasets, they've achieved superior performance while maintaining cost efficiency and full control over their models.

Industry observers note that the most significant advantage teams report is speed to value. Instead of spending weeks setting up training infrastructure or months training models from scratch, they can identify promising starting points from the community and have specialized models running in production within days.

Recent findings suggest that cost efficiency is another major benefit. By starting with models that already have relevant capabilities, teams need fewer training epochs and can use smaller datasets to achieve their target performance, dramatically reducing compute costs.

Perhaps most importantly, this approach gives teams access to the collective intelligence of the open-source community. Every breakthrough, every specialized adaptation, every novel architecture becomes a potential starting point for their own work.

As expected with a large feature of this nature, we're actively improving the experience based on real usage, so your feedback directly shapes the platform!
